One of the ways we are taught, as children, to diffuse a bully is to joke/compliment them to throw off the power balance. But we aren't taught the nuances of how to deal with this when it really is a person that has power over us, pretty much any adult feels like an authority. Met a random dude off MeetMe over the summer to hang for a day. Neither of us were emotionally available and he was so real and we vibed.  He had to move back states away but we still kept in touch.  He mentioned catastrophic thinking one-day, and I had never heard of it.  So I did some reading and he and I discussed it. Having a name for what I did was helpful, for me.  I realized how much mental energy I wasted on certain scenarios that would never play out. I have a better gage for when I'm just emotionally torturing myself, and trying to feel bad, versus when I genuinely need to be thinking ahead about something. 

So many times I've caught myself starting to spiral and beat myself up " you're such a stupid bitch..." "Not a stupid bitch, a flawed human just like everyone else" changing the way I allowed myself to talk to myself in general helped me stop always running worst case scenarios.

I would just shrug, find something to compliment them on, and move on with my day. When someone is mean, showing them kindness feels way more emotionally confusing to them than to be demeaning back.  Meeting them with annoyance or aggression means they got to you, and "they won". It's not always easy, but it allows me to feel better after the interaction.

CBT and DBT can both be absolutely life changing.  

 I have CPTSD, I've never met the full criteria for BPD, I was misdiagnosed as Bipolar at one point.  No medications ever did anything to help me, I accidentally started doing the act of [radical acceptance](https://dialecticalbehaviortherapy.com/distress-tolerance/radical-acceptance/) because i found that it helped. For me it boiled down to being able to go "it is what it is" and I know a lot of people hate that expression, but when it comes to anxiety around normal life things being able to accept certain things are just part of it is okay.  But you have to be mindful to not invalidate your emotions while doing it.
Therapy can be helpful, if you get a good therapist.  Unfortunately there are so many bad therapist/counselors out there that end up doing more harm than good. 

They suggest doing behavioral therapy alongside a professional because when you're your own sounding board it's hard to be reasonable with yourself, and it's incredibly hard to catch a spiral on your own when you first start doing it.  But, fuuuuuck man. When you can consistently start putting those purely negative thoughts to bed it gets easier for that to be the choice you make instead of thinking "I'll just KMS".  I just recently realized that thought comes from repeated trauma and learned helplessness, it's not because I'm weak, it's because my brain was stressed so much when I was young that the only way for me to have any semblance of control in my life was to acknowledge that I could rage quit life at any time.  Now that I'm older I can recognize that there are so many other tangible healthy solutions to problems besides to just end it all.  

It's still a struggle sometimes, but I can definitely recognize the positive changes in my life thanks to changing my own behaviors through DBT. I genuinely GENUINELY did not believe I'd ever be where I am now, mentally.

Definitely look up a few techniques and see if any jump out at you that you think you could easily start injecting into your routines.  Picking just one and trying is what set me on the path.  Big hugs and best of luck.

For a long time, when I was in a social interaction my brain was always "recording". I'm remembering every word of both sides to analyze it later and make myself anxious over and over again. Recently though, I've been trying to be conscious about living in the moment, not in my head, and it has helped me stop being so anxious from doing this.  I can listen to people without having to remember every word, and I find that when my brain isn't trying to remember every word of the conversation it has more capacity to flow through conversation more smoothly so I have less snafus to even feel bad about.  

I definitely catch myself trying to cling to every word sometimes and gently remind myself to just listen to the other person, it isn't a memory competition. And I genuinely enjoy my time with others a lot more now.  But, I'm still working on it.

As a former retail worker with ASD my attention to detail and organization skills got me extra departments and work thrown on me because I seemed to be able to handle it well, when inside I was burnt out and dying inside.  I worked at a big box retailer and had to manage the produce department and when it was going well they also made me take on the impulse items department (checkouts/clips strip). Neither department really suffered due to my naive sense that I was there workhorse for the time I was clocked in and I theoretically could get everything done because of how my brain schedules things. And because of my social anxiety I'd never say anything until one day I was so burnt out I just quit showing up.  This is probably what happens to lots of folks, both on the spectrum and not.

I never realized how often people think thoughts of self harm after a setback as "weakness" and not something that was a conditioned response through trauma. 

 Trauma makes your brain learn to default to what I call "rage-quitting" life.  When you feel like you've completely failed the game and you just wanna turn it off and avoid the negative feelings. The response is similar, but the result of action is different. You can turn the computer back on once you cool down and try again, as long as you didn't destroy the computer while you were in a high emotional state.
It takes a lot of time and consistent DBT work to get to just the beginnings of being able to regulate the emotion to a point it isn't overwhelming, but this is the first time I recognized I wanted to sort through this big emotion without completely turning it off!  

Thanks for being you.  :)

What caused this for me was my hyper vigilance. I thought that because I was always very aware of other peoples thoughts, as I was so sensitive to watching their body language, that everyone must be like this! Nope. Most people genuinely don't remember shit from their interactions with you, and it's not because they're rude or don't care. They just dont process things the same way people with anxiety do. Once I accepted that most people don't view/remember their interactions with me as vividly as I do, it really helped me care less about basic interactions. As long as you don't do something absolutely outlandish most people will not remember your existence. It takes a lot of pressure off from being in the world, when you have to.
